newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Chief in unusual dialogue with U.S. critics.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Chief in unusual dialogue with U.S. critics.

text.p: The new U.N. secretary-general Kofi Annan agreed to an unusual dialogue with his harshest critics in Congress in an effort to pry loose the huge United States debt to the world body.

After a warm welcome from U.S. President Bill Clinton and other members of the administration on Thursday, Annan spent close to two hours with the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and its chairman, Senator Jesse Helms, who is in the forefront of refusing payment of the $1.3 billion the United States owes.
While sceptical, Helms and a dozen other Senators were eager to talk to Annan and left the door open for some kind of payments to the United Nations. Several had their pictures taken with him.

Helms, a North Carolina Republican, said he was working on legislation that would set "benchmarks" or conditions for the payment of the debt and that Annan's staff would confer with committee staffers on the nature and pace of the reform.

"If reforms are piecemeal, if the status quo persists, then you will have a very difficult time convincing Congress to send more American tax dollars to the United Nations," he told Annan in his opening remarks. "The ball is in your court."

Usually, a United Nations secretary-general works only through the executive branch of a government and Annan earlier in the day indicated that he could not deal with parliaments of 185 member states in the world body.
But a U.N. official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Clinton had given the green light for Annan to talk to Congress regularly, which must approve any U.N. funds.

"We as a matter of protocol deal with the administration. But the administration has more or less told us go make contact with Congress and help sell the idea of the United Nations," said the official.
But he said Annan was "uncomfortable" with benchmarks but he told Helms that "if legislation was going to be introduced soon we should talk now."

Annan, a 58-year old Ghanaian career U.N. official, began his five year term Jan. 1. He was strongly supported by the Clinton administration, which single-handedly blocked a second term for Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt for allegedly not doing enough to reform the world body.
At the White House, Clinton in a joint appearance with Annan told reporters: "As long as the United Nations does its part, we should simply be prepared to pay our debts and pay our dues."
He said putting the U.N. back on a sound financial footing demanded "far-reaching reform, the elimination of waste, streamlining staff, wiping out overlap and abuse."
Annan said if the United Nations did not change it would lose its relevance. Simply put, what the United Nations wants is what the U.S. also wants: a reformed United Nations.
The secretary-general has also made clear that reform meant efficiency and not necessarily what one U.N. official called "a slash and burn" approach cutting costs.

While no "benchmarks" were revealed by Helms, one of them was bound to be a cut in the U.S. assessment to 20 percent from 25 percent. Dues are based on a country's economic wealth, which puts the United States at 27 percent.
With the United States lagging in its payments, the United Nations is kept afloat largely by the European Union countries and Japan, who together pay well over 50 percent.

Annan since he took office has promised numerous times to present a programme for restructuring the world body by July and present it to members for approval. Any such plans are fraught with difficulties since many U.N. agencies set standards that could favour or injure one industry or one country.
At the same time, Annan, officials said, was faced with questions that U.N. officials considered gross misconceptions spurred by right-wing think tanks.

One was proposals from academics that various taxes be imposed to finance the United Nations, an idea that has never been seriously discussed in the world body. Annan, his aides said, had to deny that he advocated such a plan or that United Nations staff had published books on it.
